questions.text: A developer must upload a local file `report.csv` from his Linux session into the HDFS directory `/data/reports`. Which command is correct?
options: `hdfs dfs -ls /data/reports report.csv`
`hdfs dfs -put ./report.csv /data/reports`
`hdfs dfs -cat report.csv > /data/reports`
`hdfs dfs -rm ./report.csv /data/reports`
`hdfs dfs -mkdir ./report.csv /data/reports`
questions.shortExplanation: `hdfs dfs -put` uploads a local file into an HDFS directory.
questions.explanation: The `-put` sub-command is the standard way to copy a local file from the Linux filesystem into HDFS. The first argument is the local source path and the second is the HDFS destination directory or file path. The NameNode allocates blocks, the DataNodes form the replication pipeline, and the file appears under the given HDFS path. The very similar `-copyFromLocal` does the same job, while `-get` and `-copyToLocal` go in the opposite direction. `-ls` only lists, `-cat` prints contents to stdout, `-rm` deletes, and `-mkdir` creates a directory, so none of them upload a file from the local disk into HDFS.

questions.text: A DevOps engineer is auditing how many blocks a file has, with their locations, for `/Installer/my_install.log`. Which command provides BOTH block info and block locations?
options: `hdfs dfs -ls -files -blocks /Installer/my_install.log`
`hdfs fsck /Installer/my_install.log -files -blocks -locations`
`hdfs dfs -count /Installer/my_install.log`
`hdfs dfs -du /Installer/my_install.log`
`hdfs dfs -tail /Installer/my_install.log`
questions.shortExplanation: `hdfs fsck <path> -files -blocks -locations` shows blocks and where they live.
questions.explanation: The `hdfs fsck` utility checks the health of files in HDFS and reports block-level information. The `-files` flag lists the file, `-blocks` shows the list of blocks that make it up, and `-locations` adds the DataNode addresses where each block replica is stored. Combined, these flags give a complete picture of how a file is distributed across the cluster, which is exactly what a DevOps engineer needs for auditing. `-ls`, `-count`, `-du`, and `-tail` show listings, counts, sizes, or the last bytes of a file, but none of them expose block IDs or DataNode locations.

questions.text: A team wants to upload `large.log` to HDFS but force a non-default block size of 1 MB (1048576 bytes) for that particular file only. Which command is correct?
options: `hdfs dfs -put ./large.log /data -blocksize=1048576`
`hdfs dfs -D dfs.blocksize=1048576 -put ./large.log /data`
`hdfs dfs -set dfs.blocksize=1048576 -put ./large.log /data`
`hdfs config blocksize 1048576 /data/large.log`
`hdfs dfs -mkdir -D dfs.blocksize=1048576 /data/large.log`
questions.shortExplanation: Pass `-D dfs.blocksize=<bytes>` to the put command to override block size for one file.
questions.explanation: The Hadoop CLI accepts generic properties using the `-D` flag, which sets a configuration value for that command only. To force a non-default block size on a single upload, write `hdfs dfs -D dfs.blocksize=<bytes> -put <local> <hdfs>`. The cluster's default `dfs.blocksize` stays unchanged, and only the file uploaded by this command uses the custom size, which is useful for small files or special tuning. The other options invent flags like `-blocksize=`, `-set`, or `hdfs config` that do not exist in the HDFS CLI, or apply the option to `-mkdir` which does not write data, so they are all wrong.

questions.text: An analyst loads a file `hive_table.txt` (tab-separated id and name) already placed in HDFS at `/Class-2/hive/hive_table.txt`. Which Hive command correctly creates and loads a MANAGED table?
options: `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE hive_table(id INT, Name STRING); LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH '/Class-2/hive/hive_table.txt' INTO TABLE hive_table;`
`CREATE TABLE hive_table(id INT, Name STRING) ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'; LOAD DATA INPATH '/Class-2/hive/hive_table.txt' INTO TABLE hive_table;`
`INSERT TABLE hive_table FROM '/Class-2/hive/hive_table.txt';`
`COPY hive_table FROM '/Class-2/hive/hive_table.txt' DELIMITER '\t';`
`BULK LOAD hive_table INFILE '/Class-2/hive/hive_table.txt';`
questions.shortExplanation: Use `CREATE TABLE ... ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY` and then `LOAD DATA INPATH` for a managed table.
questions.explanation: A managed Hive table is created with plain `CREATE TABLE`, no EXTERNAL keyword, and the schema lists each column with its type. `ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'` tells Hive that fields are tab-separated. Because the source file is already in HDFS, `LOAD DATA INPATH` (without LOCAL) moves it into the managed table's warehouse directory. From then on, Hive owns the data and will delete it if the table is dropped. EXTERNAL tables leave data out of Hive's control, and INSERT TABLE FROM, COPY FROM, or BULK LOAD INFILE are not valid HiveQL commands, so those options are wrong.

questions.text: A developer wants Hive to create dynamic partitions when inserting from a non-partitioned table `All_Pakistan` into a partitioned table `Pak_part` (partitioned by `Province`). Which setting must be applied BEFORE the INSERT?
options: `SET hive.mapred.mode = strict;`
`SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;`
`SET hive.enforce.bucketing = false;`
`SET hive.partition.disable = true;`
`SET hive.dynamic = off;`
questions.shortExplanation: `SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;` enables dynamic partitioning for the INSERT.
questions.explanation: Before an INSERT that wants Hive to create partitions automatically from a source column, the session must allow nonstrict dynamic partitioning. The command `SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;` removes the requirement that at least one partition column be static. With dynamic partitioning enabled, Hive reads each row, looks at the partition column value, and writes the row into the matching partition directory. Setting strict mode blocks fully dynamic inserts, disabling bucketing is unrelated, and properties like `hive.partition.disable` or `hive.dynamic=off` are made up, so those options will not work.

questions.text: In Pig, a team wants to load `/drivers.csv` (comma-separated) and project only `driverId` ($0) and `name` ($1). Which Pig Latin sequence is correct?
options: `drivers = READ '/drivers.csv' DELIMITER ','; SELECT $0, $1 FROM drivers;`
`drivers = LOAD '/drivers.csv' USING PigStorage(','); each_driver = FOREACH drivers GENERATE $0 AS driverId, $1 AS name;`
`drivers = OPEN '/drivers.csv'; FOREACH drivers PROJECT $0, $1;`
`LOAD drivers FROM '/drivers.csv'; PROJECT $0, $1 INTO each_driver;`
`drivers = IMPORT '/drivers.csv'; each_driver = FILTER drivers BY $0, $1;`
questions.shortExplanation: Use `LOAD ... USING PigStorage(',')` then `FOREACH ... GENERATE $0, $1` to project columns.
questions.explanation: Pig reads delimited files with `LOAD '<path>' USING PigStorage(',')`, where PigStorage tells Pig the field separator. The result is a relation of tuples whose positional columns are accessed as `$0`, `$1`, and so on. To project only the first two columns and rename them, use `FOREACH drivers GENERATE $0 AS driverId, $1 AS name;`. This is the standard load-then-project pattern in Pig Latin. Commands like READ, OPEN, IMPORT, PROJECT, or SELECT are not Pig Latin keywords, and FILTER is used for predicates not projection, so those options will not parse.

questions.text: A Pig script must SUM miles per driver. After `group_data = GROUP time_sheet BY driverId;`, which FOREACH expression aggregates miles correctly?
options: `sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, COUNT(time_sheet.miles_logged);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, SUM(time_sheet.miles_logged);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE AVG(time_sheet);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE FILTER(miles_logged);`
`sum_data = FOREACH time_sheet GENERATE SUM(group_data);`
questions.shortExplanation: After GROUP BY, use `FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, SUM(time_sheet.miles_logged)` to total miles.
questions.explanation: When a Pig relation is grouped, each row of the result has a `group` field with the key and an inner bag named after the original relation. To sum a column across that bag, use the SUM aggregate inside a FOREACH, like `SUM(time_sheet.miles_logged)`. The output gives one row per driver with their total miles, which is what the aggregation requires. COUNT only counts rows, AVG computes mean not sum, FILTER does not aggregate, and applying SUM to the original ungrouped relation does not produce per-driver totals.

questions.text: A backend engineer wants to implement the standard "read-through cache" pattern using Redis in front of a relational database. A request arrives for `user:123`. Which sequence correctly describes the application logic?
options: Always read from DB first, then optionally update Redis on a background thread
Look up the key `user:123` in Redis. On HIT, return the cached value. On MISS, fetch from the DB, store the result back in Redis (with a TTL), and return the data
Bypass Redis on every read; use it only for writes
Read both Redis and the DB in parallel and return whichever responds last
Invalidate Redis on every read regardless of HIT/MISS
questions.shortExplanation: Read-through cache: check Redis first; on HIT return it, on MISS read DB, write back to Redis, return.
questions.explanation: The read-through pattern wraps every read in a small piece of logic. The app first asks Redis for the key. If Redis returns a value (HIT), the app uses it immediately. If Redis says the key is missing (MISS), the app queries the relational DB, writes the result back into Redis with a TTL, and returns it to the caller. Subsequent reads of the same key now hit Redis and avoid the DB, which is exactly the goal of caching. Always reading DB first, bypassing Redis, reading both in parallel, or invalidating on every read all defeat the purpose of a cache and would lose its latency benefits.

questions.text: A team caches product details in Redis but a stale catalog is being shown to customers after a price update in the DB. Which Redis best-practice combination addresses this stale-data problem?
options: Disable Redis entirely and serve all reads from the DB
Set an appropriate TTL (Time-To-Live) for the cached key AND invalidate/update the cache entry whenever the underlying DB row changes (e.g., via change-event triggers or Pub/Sub)
Never invalidate cache; let the data drift naturally
Use Redis only as a write-only store
Lower the TTL so far that every request becomes a miss, effectively bypassing the cache
questions.shortExplanation: Set a TTL on cached keys AND invalidate or update them when the DB row changes.
questions.explanation: Stale cache happens when the DB is updated but Redis still holds the old value. The fix is two-fold. First, every cached key gets a Time-To-Live so it expires and is naturally refreshed after a known window. Second, when the underlying DB row changes, the app or a change-event hook (such as a Pub/Sub trigger) invalidates or updates the corresponding Redis key right away. Together these keep the cache from drifting too far from the source of truth. Disabling Redis kills its benefit, never invalidating guarantees stale data, write-only Redis is meaningless for reads, and a TTL of zero turns every request into a miss and removes the cache.

questions.text: A real-time analytics team must build a publish-subscribe pipeline where order events are split into partitions for horizontal scalability, each consumer group receives every message once, and ZooKeeper handles leader election. Which technology stack fits this architecture and what does each component do?
options: Use RabbitMQ — producers post directly to consumers without partitions

Use Apache Kafka — producers send to topics (partitioned for scalability), brokers store the data and replicate it across the cluster for fault tolerance, consumer groups read with once-only processing per message, and ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata and leader election
Use Redis — Redis is a stream-only system with no partitions
Use Kubernetes — Kubernetes is a messaging system
Use MongoDB ACID transactions as the message bus
questions.shortExplanation: Kafka topics are partitioned for scale, brokers replicate them, consumer groups read once per message, ZooKeeper coordinates brokers.
questions.explanation: Producers publish events into named Kafka topics, and each topic is divided into partitions so messages can be spread across brokers for horizontal scalability. Brokers store the partition logs and replicate them across the cluster so a broker failure does not lose data. Consumers join a consumer group, and each partition is assigned to one consumer in the group, which gives exactly-once-per-group processing. ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata, leader election, and consumer offsets in older versions. RabbitMQ has no partitions, Redis is not a partitioned event log, Kubernetes is not a messaging system, and MongoDB ACID is a database, so none of them match this architecture.

questions.text: A web app generates PDF invoices that are too slow to produce inline. The team decides to offload the work via RabbitMQ. Which sequence correctly describes the RabbitMQ workflow per the slides?
options: Producer (web app) → Queue → Exchange → Consumer (worker)
Producer (web app) sends a message to an Exchange, which routes it (via bindings/routing keys) to a Queue, where it waits until a Consumer (worker) connects and processes it
Consumer pushes the message directly to the Producer
The Queue produces messages and sends them to the Exchange
There is no broker — producer and consumer communicate directly
questions.shortExplanation: RabbitMQ flow: Producer → Exchange → (routing rules) → Queue → Consumer.
questions.explanation: In RabbitMQ, a producer never sends messages directly to a queue. It publishes to an Exchange and includes a routing key or attributes. The exchange uses its bindings (direct, topic, fanout, headers) to decide which queues should receive the message. A consumer subscribes to one of those queues and processes messages as they arrive. This decoupling allows the producer to be unaware of which workers will handle the work. Other orderings, having the consumer push back to the producer, or claiming there is no broker contradict how RabbitMQ actually routes messages.

questions.text: A senior architect is asked to choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ for a new system that needs FLEXIBLE message routing — direct, topic, fanout — and is primarily about reliably distributing work to specific worker queues (PDF generation, email sending) rather than retaining a long event log for replay. Which is the better fit and why?
options: Kafka — because Kafka has Exchanges and is built for task queues
RabbitMQ — it is a message broker with Exchanges and bindings supporting flexible routing patterns, ideal for decoupling producer/consumer for async task distribution
Both are equivalent and the choice doesn't matter
Neither — only Redis Pub/Sub fits this use case
Use Kubernetes since it routes messages natively
questions.shortExplanation: Pick RabbitMQ when you need flexible exchange-based routing and reliable async task delivery.
questions.explanation: RabbitMQ is the right tool for systems where work must be reliably handed off from producers to specific worker queues, and where routing rules vary by message type. Exchanges support direct, topic, and fanout routing patterns that let one publish reach exactly the queues that need it. It is not built to retain a long event log for replay, which is what Kafka is for. PDF generation and bulk email sending are textbook RabbitMQ workloads. Kafka does not use exchanges, claiming the two are equivalent ignores their core design difference, Redis Pub/Sub does not give durable task delivery, and Kubernetes does not route application messages.

questions.text: A fintech app processes a money transfer: it must (1) debit account A, (2) credit account B, and (3) write an audit row — all three or none. The team wraps the three writes inside a MongoDB multi-document ACID transaction. The "or none" guarantee in this scenario is provided by which ACID property?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity — all operations succeed together or none are applied; partial updates are prevented
Durability
Availability
questions.shortExplanation: Atomicity guarantees that all operations in a transaction succeed together or none are applied.
questions.explanation: In a MongoDB multi-document transaction, Atomicity treats the whole transaction as one indivisible unit. Either every write inside it commits, or if anything fails the database rolls back all of them, leaving the data exactly as it was before. This stops half-finished outcomes such as a debit without a credit, which would corrupt account balances. Atomicity is enforced through the commit and abort protocol around the wrapped operations. Consistency is about constraints, Isolation is about concurrent visibility, Durability is about surviving crashes after commit, and Availability is not even an ACID property, so they do not describe all-or-nothing behavior.

questions.text: The same fintech team is told that, after `commitTransaction()` returns success, the changes must persist even if the database server power-cycles immediately afterwards. Which ACID property guarantees this and how should it be reasoned about in MongoDB?
options: Atomicity — because the operation was indivisible
Isolation — because no other transaction can see partial state
Durability — once a transaction commits successfully, its effects are persisted permanently and survive crashes/restarts/power failures
Consistency — because the constraints were valid
Partition Tolerance — because the network kept working
questions.shortExplanation: Durability means the committed transaction's effects survive crashes, restarts, and power failures.
questions.explanation: Once `commitTransaction()` returns success in MongoDB, Durability promises that the change is now safely on disk in the journal and replicas. Even if the server power-cycles a millisecond later, the data is recovered on restart. MongoDB achieves this with journaling and write-concern majority, which forces the commit to be acknowledged on multiple nodes before returning success. Without Durability, a successful commit could be lost, breaking trust in the system. Atomicity is about indivisibility, Isolation is about concurrent access, Consistency is about constraints, and Partition Tolerance belongs to CAP not ACID, so they do not describe crash survival of committed data.

questions.text: A DevOps engineer writes a Kubernetes manifest in YAML that declares "3 replicas of nginx with image nginx:1.25." After applying it, one Pod gets killed. The system automatically starts a new Pod to maintain 3 replicas. Which TWO Kubernetes capabilities does this scenario MOST directly illustrate?
options: Declarative configuration (desired state in YAML) + Self-healing (controller reconciles actual state to desired state)
Manual SSH + Hard-coded IP routing
Vertical scaling + Static IP assignment
Database replication + Cache eviction
Kafka partitioning + RabbitMQ exchanges
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes uses declarative YAML for desired state and a self-healing controller loop to maintain it.
questions.explanation: A Kubernetes manifest expresses what the user wants — for example, three replicas of an nginx Pod — and submits it to the API Server. Controllers then continuously compare the actual cluster state to that desired state. If a Pod dies, the ReplicaSet controller notices the mismatch and starts a new Pod automatically, bringing the count back to three. This combination of declarative configuration and a self-healing reconcile loop is the heart of how Kubernetes operates. Manual SSH, hard-coded IPs, vertical scaling only, plain DB replication, or Kafka and RabbitMQ features are not what this YAML-plus-controller behavior demonstrates.

questions.text: A microservices team deploys 20 services on Kubernetes. As traffic grows, they need new instances to spin up automatically and have traffic routed to them without manually editing config files. Which Kubernetes features address this?
options: Manual port-forwarding and hand-edited hosts files
Horizontal scaling (add Pods/Nodes) combined with Service Discovery and Load Balancing — services locate each other dynamically and traffic is distributed across replicas
Vertical scaling only — adding RAM to a single Pod
Disable autoscaling and rely on a single replica per service
Move everything off Kubernetes and back onto bare VMs
questions.shortExplanation: Horizontal scaling plus Service Discovery and Load Balancing let new Pods receive traffic automatically.
questions.explanation: When a microservice needs more capacity, Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can add more Pods. Each Service object gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP that automatically tracks the set of healthy Pods behind it. kube-proxy programs network rules so that traffic to the service is load-balanced across all current replicas. New Pods are discovered and added to the rotation without anyone editing config files by hand. Manual port-forwarding, single-replica setups, vertical-only scaling, and moving off Kubernetes all defeat the very automation the team is trying to use.

questions.text: A team wants Redis to remain available and absorb more traffic than a single instance can handle (100K req/sec is the target). Which Redis scaling strategy from the slides matches this requirement?
options: Vertical scaling only — buy a bigger single Redis server
Use Redis Clusters or replication to distribute data across multiple instances and increase throughput
Run Redis on a single laptop in development mode
Disable Redis and use a relational DB instead
Use Kafka instead of Redis since Redis cannot scale
questions.shortExplanation: Use Redis Clusters or replication to spread data and serve more than a single instance can handle.
questions.explanation: A single Redis instance has a CPU and memory ceiling, so to push beyond it Redis offers two scaling tools. Redis Cluster shards keys across multiple primary nodes, increasing throughput and capacity together. Replication adds replicas to a primary so read traffic can be served from several nodes and failover is possible if the primary dies. Together they let Redis scale horizontally to hundreds of thousands of requests per second. Sticking to one bigger server eventually hits the same ceiling, dev-mode laptops are toys, replacing Redis with an RDBMS loses the low-latency benefit, and Kafka is not a cache replacement.

questions.text: A Kafka consumer group is processing the `orders` topic. The team wants to REPLAY messages from a point earlier than where the group is currently positioned, to recover from a downstream bug. Which Kafka concept makes this possible?
options: Kafka messages are deleted instantly after consumption, so replay is impossible
Consumers can choose any OFFSET to start reading from within the topic's retention window — Kafka retains messages for a configured period, enabling replay
Only Kafka producers can read past messages, not consumers
RabbitMQ must be installed alongside Kafka to enable replay
Replay requires shutting down the entire Kafka cluster
questions.shortExplanation: Kafka retains messages for a configured period and lets consumers seek to any offset within it to replay.
questions.explanation: Each Kafka topic partition is an append-only log where every message has an offset. Kafka keeps the messages for as long as the retention configuration allows, regardless of whether anyone has consumed them. A consumer can rewind its committed offset, or set a fresh starting offset such as `earliest`, to replay past messages and reprocess them — which is how teams recover from downstream bugs without producing the events again. Saying Kafka deletes messages instantly, restricting reads to producers, claiming RabbitMQ is required, or demanding a full cluster shutdown all contradict how Kafka offsets and retention actually work.

questions.text: A startup runs a banking application requiring strong consistency and rollback on failure, plus a social-media-feed service prioritizing availability and tolerating eventual consistency. Which architecture pairing is correct per the ACID-vs-BASE comparison in the slides?
options: Banking → BASE database; Feed → ACID database
Banking → ACID database (strong consistency, transactional rollback, durability); Feed → BASE system (eventual consistency, high availability, relaxed durability)
Both should use BASE because ACID is impossible in distributed systems
Both should use ACID since BASE is unsafe under any condition
Banking → no DB at all; Feed → ACID only
questions.shortExplanation: Use ACID for strong, consistent transactional systems and BASE for highly available, eventually consistent feeds.
questions.explanation: ACID databases give strong consistency, transactional rollback, and durability, which is exactly what a banking application needs so it never shows partial transfers. BASE systems prioritize availability and partition tolerance, accepting that replicas may briefly disagree before converging — perfect for a social-media feed where users tolerate seeing slightly stale posts in exchange for the service never being down. Choosing the right side per workload is a core distributed-systems decision. Swapping the two would put feed data on a slow strict system and money on an eventually consistent one, and claims like 'ACID is impossible' or 'BASE is unsafe' overstate the trade-off.

questions.text: A Kubernetes cluster has a Control Plane and three Worker Nodes. Each Worker Node runs Pods, plus two helper components. Which two components run on EACH Worker Node, and what do they do (per the K8s architecture slide)?
options: API Server (handles requests) and etcd (stores cluster state)
kubelet (manages the Pods on the node, talks to the control plane) and kube-proxy (handles network rules and service routing for Pods)
Scheduler (places Pods) and Controller Manager (reconciles state)
ZooKeeper and Kafka Broker
Redis Cluster and RabbitMQ Exchange
questions.shortExplanation: Each Worker Node runs `kubelet` (manages Pods on the node) and `kube-proxy` (handles network routing for services).
questions.explanation: On every Kubernetes Worker Node two helper components run alongside the user Pods. The `kubelet` talks to the control plane, starts and supervises containers in Pods, and reports node and Pod health back to the API Server. `kube-proxy` programs the node's iptables or IPVS rules so traffic for a Service is correctly load-balanced to the right Pod IPs. Together they implement the worker side of the Kubernetes architecture. API Server, etcd, Scheduler, and Controller Manager are control-plane components, while ZooKeeper, Kafka, Redis, and RabbitMQ are entirely different products, so none of them run on a Worker Node by default.

questions.text: A Hive developer wants to dynamically create partitions when inserting from a non-partitioned table `Sales_Raw` into a partitioned table `Sales_Part` partitioned by `Region`. Which session setting must be applied BEFORE the INSERT?

With dynamic partitioning enabled, Hive reads each row, looks at the partition column value, and writes the row into the matching partition directory. Setting strict mode blocks fully dynamic inserts, disabling bucketing is unrelated, and properties like `hive.partition.disable` or `hive.dynamic=off` are made up, so those options will not work.

questions.text: In Pig, a developer needs to load `/employees.csv` (comma-separated) and project only `empId` ($0) and `empName` ($1). Which Pig Latin sequence is correct?

questions.text: A backend developer wants the standard "read-through cache" pattern using Redis in front of PostgreSQL. A request arrives for `product:567`. Which logic correctly captures the pattern?

Look up `product:567` in Redis; on HIT return cached value; on MISS read from PostgreSQL, write the result back to Redis with a TTL, and return the data
Bypass Redis on every read and use it only for writes
Read Redis and PostgreSQL in parallel and return whichever responds last
Invalidate the Redis key on every read regardless of HIT/MISS
questions.shortExplanation: Read-through cache: check Redis first; on HIT return it, on MISS read DB, write back to Redis, return.
questions.explanation: The read-through pattern wraps every read in a small piece of logic. The app first asks Redis for the key. If Redis returns a value (HIT), the app uses it immediately. If Redis says the key is missing (MISS), the app queries the relational DB, writes the result back into Redis with a TTL, and returns it to the caller. Subsequent reads of the same key now hit Redis and avoid the DB, which is exactly the goal of caching. Always reading DB first, bypassing Redis, reading both in parallel, or invalidating on every read all defeat the purpose of a cache and would lose its latency benefits.

questions.text: After a price change in the source DB, customers continue to see the old price from Redis. Which Redis best-practice combination resolves this stale-data issue?

Set an appropriate TTL for the cached key AND invalidate/update the cache entry when the underlying DB row changes (e.g., change-event triggers or Pub/Sub notifications)
Never invalidate; let data naturally drift
Use Redis only as a write-only store
Lower the TTL so far that every request becomes a miss, effectively bypassing the cache
questions.shortExplanation: Set a TTL on cached keys AND invalidate or update them when the DB row changes.
questions.explanation: Stale cache happens when the DB is updated but Redis still holds the old value. The fix is two-fold. First, every cached key gets a Time-To-Live so it expires and is naturally refreshed after a known window. Second, when the underlying DB row changes, the app or a change-event hook (such as a Pub/Sub trigger) invalidates or updates the corresponding Redis key right away. Together these keep the cache from drifting too far from the source of truth. Disabling Redis kills its benefit, never invalidating guarantees stale data, write-only Redis is meaningless for reads, and a TTL of zero turns every request into a miss and removes the cache.

questions.text: A real-time analytics platform needs a pub-sub pipeline where transaction events are partitioned for horizontal scalability, every consumer group receives each message exactly once, ZooKeeper handles leader election, and messages survive broker failure via replication. Which technology stack fits and what is each component's role?

Redis — Redis is a stream-only system with no partitions
Kubernetes — Kubernetes is the underlying messaging system
MongoDB ACID transactions as the message bus
questions.shortExplanation: Kafka topics are partitioned for scale, brokers replicate them, consumer groups read once per message, ZooKeeper coordinates brokers.
questions.explanation: Producers publish events into named Kafka topics, and each topic is divided into partitions so messages can be spread across brokers for horizontal scalability. Brokers store the partition logs and replicate them across the cluster so a broker failure does not lose data. Consumers join a consumer group, and each partition is assigned to one consumer in the group, which gives exactly-once-per-group processing. ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata, leader election, and consumer offsets in older versions. RabbitMQ has no partitions, Redis is not a partitioned event log, Kubernetes is not a messaging system, and MongoDB ACID is a database, so none of them match this architecture.

questions.text: A web app must offload bulk email sending so user requests stay fast. The team adopts RabbitMQ. Which sequence correctly captures the RabbitMQ message flow per the slides?
options: Producer → Queue → Exchange → Consumer
Producer (web app) sends a message to an Exchange, which routes it (via bindings and routing keys) to a Queue, where it waits until a Consumer (worker) connects and processes it
Consumer pushes the message back to the Producer
The Queue produces messages and sends them to the Exchange
There is no broker — producer and consumer communicate directly
questions.shortExplanation: RabbitMQ flow: Producer → Exchange → (routing rules) → Queue → Consumer.
questions.explanation: In RabbitMQ, a producer never sends messages directly to a queue. It publishes to an Exchange and includes a routing key or attributes. The exchange uses its bindings (direct, topic, fanout, headers) to decide which queues should receive the message. A consumer subscribes to one of those queues and processes messages as they arrive. This decoupling allows the producer to be unaware of which workers will handle the work. Other orderings, having the consumer push back to the producer, or claiming there is no broker contradict how RabbitMQ actually routes messages.

questions.text: An architect must choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ for a new system that needs FLEXIBLE message routing (direct, topic, fanout) and is primarily about reliably distributing async tasks to specific worker queues rather than retaining a long event log for replay. Which fits best and why?

RabbitMQ — a message broker with Exchanges and bindings that supports flexible routing patterns, ideal for decoupling producer/consumer for async task distribution
Both are equivalent; the choice is irrelevant
Neither — only Redis Pub/Sub fits this use case
Use Kubernetes; it natively routes messages
questions.shortExplanation: Pick RabbitMQ when you need flexible exchange-based routing and reliable async task delivery.
questions.explanation: RabbitMQ is the right tool for systems where work must be reliably handed off from producers to specific worker queues, and where routing rules vary by message type. Exchanges support direct, topic, and fanout routing patterns that let one publish reach exactly the queues that need it. It is not built to retain a long event log for replay, which is what Kafka is for. PDF generation and bulk email sending are textbook RabbitMQ workloads. questions.text: A payments platform implements a transfer that must (1) debit account A, (2) credit account B, and (3) insert an audit row — all three or none. The team wraps these in a MongoDB multi-document ACID transaction. The "or none" guarantee is provided by which ACID property?

Consistency is about constraints, Isolation is about concurrent visibility, Durability is about surviving crashes after commit, and Availability is not even an ACID property, so they do not describe all-or-nothing behavior.

MongoDB achieves this with journaling and write-concern majority, which forces the commit to be acknowledged on multiple nodes before returning success. questions.text: A DevOps engineer writes a Kubernetes manifest in YAML declaring "4 replicas of api-server with image api:2.0". After applying it, one Pod is killed by an OOM event. Disable autoscaling and rely on a single replica per service
Move everything off Kubernetes and back onto bare VMs

New Pods are discovered and added to the rotation without anyone editing config files by hand. Manual port-forwarding, single-replica setups, vertical-only scaling, and moving off Kubernetes all defeat the very automation the team is trying to use.

questions.text: A team needs Redis to absorb >250K req/sec — more than one instance can handle. Which Redis scaling strategy aligns with what was taught?
options: Vertical scaling only — buy a bigger Redis box
Use Redis Clusters or replication to distribute data across multiple instances and increase throughput
Run Redis on a developer laptop in dev mode
Disable Redis and use a relational DB instead
Use Kafka instead of Redis, because Redis cannot scale
questions.shortExplanation: Use Redis Clusters or replication to spread data and serve more than a single instance can handle.
questions.explanation: A single Redis instance has a CPU and memory ceiling, so to push beyond it Redis offers two scaling tools. Redis Cluster shards keys across multiple primary nodes, increasing throughput and capacity together. Replication adds replicas to a primary so read traffic can be served from several nodes and failover is possible if the primary dies. Together they let Redis scale horizontally to hundreds of thousands of requests per second. Sticking to one bigger server eventually hits the same ceiling, dev-mode laptops are toys, replacing Redis with an RDBMS loses the low-latency benefit, and Kafka is not a cache replacement.

questions.text: A Kafka consumer group on the `payments` topic must REPLAY messages from an earlier point to recover from a downstream bug introduced last hour. Which Kafka concept makes this possible?
options: Kafka deletes messages immediately on consumption, so replay is impossible
Consumers can choose any OFFSET to start reading from within the topic's retention window — Kafka retains messages for a configured period, enabling replay
Only Kafka producers can read past messages, not consumers
RabbitMQ must be installed alongside Kafka to enable replay
Replay requires shutting down the entire Kafka cluster

questions.explanation: Each Kafka topic partition is an append-only log where every message has an offset. questions.text: A startup launches a stock-trading platform requiring strong consistency and rollback on failure, plus a feed-of-likes service that prioritizes availability and tolerates eventual consistency. Which architectural pairing matches the ACID-vs-BASE comparison taught?

Trading → no DB; Likes → ACID only

questions.explanation: ACID databases give strong consistency, transactional rollback, and durability, which is exactly what a banking application needs so it never shows partial transfers. questions.text: A Kubernetes cluster has a Control Plane plus four Worker Nodes. Each Worker Node runs Pods plus two helper components. Which TWO components run on EACH Worker Node, and what do they do (per the K8s architecture taught)?

ZooKeeper and Kafka Broker
Redis Cluster and RabbitMQ Exchange

questions.explanation: On every Kubernetes Worker Node two helper components run alongside the user Pods. The `kubelet` talks to the control plane, starts and supervises containers in Pods, and reports node and Pod health back to the API Server. `kube-proxy` programs the node's iptables or IPVS rules so traffic for a Service is correctly load-balanced to the right Pod IPs. `hdfs dfs -count /logs/app.log`

`hdfs dfs -tail /logs/app.log`

questions.text: A DevOps engineer writes a Kubernetes YAML manifest declaring "5 replicas of web-app with image web:1.5". After applying it, one Pod is evicted due to a node drain. Kubernetes immediately starts a new Pod on another node to maintain 5 replicas. Which TWO K8s capabilities does this MOST directly illustrate?

Manual SSH + Hand-edited routing tables
Vertical scaling + Static IP assignment
Database replication + Cache eviction
Kafka partitioning + RabbitMQ exchanges
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes uses declarative YAML for desired state and a self-healing controller loop to maintain it.
questions.explanation: A Kubernetes manifest expresses what the user wants — for example, three replicas of an nginx Pod — and submits it to the API Server. Vertical scaling only — adding RAM to a single Pod

Move everything off Kubernetes and back onto bare VMs

questions.text: A team needs Redis to absorb >500K req/sec — more than a single instance can handle. Which Redis scaling strategy aligns with what was taught?

Use Redis Clusters or replication to distribute data across multiple instances and increase throughput
Run Redis on a developer laptop in dev mode
Disable Redis and use a relational DB
Use Kafka instead of Redis since Redis cannot scale

questions.text: A Kafka consumer group on the `clicks` topic must REPLAY messages from an earlier point to rebuild a downstream cache corrupted yesterday. Which Kafka concept enables this?
options: Kafka deletes messages immediately on consumption — replay is impossible
Consumers can choose any OFFSET within the topic's retention window — Kafka retains messages for a configured period, enabling replay
Only Kafka producers can read past messages, not consumers
RabbitMQ must be installed alongside Kafka for replay
Replay requires shutting down the entire Kafka cluster

questions.text: A startup runs a securities-trading platform requiring strong consistency and rollback on failure, plus a social-share-counter service that prioritizes availability and tolerates eventual consistency. Which architectural pairing matches the ACID-vs-BASE comparison taught?

ZooKeeper and Kafka Broker
Redis Cluster and RabbitMQ Exchange

questions.text: A developer must upload `transactions.csv` from a Linux shell into the HDFS directory `/lake/transactions`. Which command is correct?
options: `hdfs dfs -ls /lake/transactions transactions.csv`
`hdfs dfs -put ./transactions.csv /lake/transactions`

`hdfs dfs -rm ./transactions.csv /lake/transactions`
`hdfs dfs -mkdir ./transactions.csv /lake/transactions`
questions.shortExplanation: `hdfs dfs -put` uploads a local file into an HDFS directory.
questions.explanation: The `-put` sub-command is the standard way to copy a local file from the Linux filesystem into HDFS. The first argument is the local source path and the second is the HDFS destination directory or file path. The NameNode allocates blocks, the DataNodes form the replication pipeline, and the file appears under the given HDFS path. The very similar `-copyFromLocal` does the same job, while `-get` and `-copyToLocal` go in the opposite direction. `-ls` only lists, `-cat` prints contents to stdout, `-rm` deletes, and `-mkdir` creates a directory, so none of them upload a file from the local disk into HDFS.

questions.text: A DevOps engineer audits the number of blocks AND their physical DataNode locations for `/audits/access.log`. Which command returns BOTH?
options: `hdfs dfs -ls -files -blocks /audits/access.log`
`hdfs fsck /audits/access.log -files -blocks -locations`
`hdfs dfs -count /audits/access.log`
`hdfs dfs -du /audits/access.log`
`hdfs dfs -tail /audits/access.log`
questions.shortExplanation: `hdfs fsck <path> -files -blocks -locations` shows blocks and where they live.
questions.explanation: The `hdfs fsck` utility checks the health of files in HDFS and reports block-level information. The `-files` flag lists the file, `-blocks` shows the list of blocks that make it up, and `-locations` adds the DataNode addresses where each block replica is stored. Combined, these flags give a complete picture of how a file is distributed across the cluster, which is exactly what a DevOps engineer needs for auditing. `-ls`, `-count`, `-du`, and `-tail` show listings, counts, sizes, or the last bytes of a file, but none of them expose block IDs or DataNode locations.

questions.text: A team uploads `journal.log` to HDFS, forcing a non-default block size of 8 MB (8388608 bytes) for that single file. Which command is correct?
options: `hdfs dfs -put ./journal.log /data -blocksize=8388608`
`hdfs dfs -D dfs.blocksize=8388608 -put ./journal.log /data`
`hdfs dfs -set dfs.blocksize=8388608 -put ./journal.log /data`
`hdfs config blocksize 8388608 /data/journal.log`
`hdfs dfs -mkdir -D dfs.blocksize=8388608 /data/journal.log`
questions.shortExplanation: Pass `-D dfs.blocksize=<bytes>` to the put command to override block size for one file.
questions.explanation: The Hadoop CLI accepts generic properties using the `-D` flag, which sets a configuration value for that command only. To force a non-default block size on a single upload, write `hdfs dfs -D dfs.blocksize=<bytes> -put <local> <hdfs>`. The other options invent flags like `-blocksize=`, `-set`, or `hdfs config` that do not exist in the HDFS CLI, or apply the option to `-mkdir` which does not write data, so they are all wrong.

questions.text: A Hive analyst has a tab-separated file `vendors.txt` (id, name) already in HDFS at `/data/hive/vendors.txt`. Which command correctly creates and loads a MANAGED Hive table?
options: `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ven(id INT, name STRING); LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH '/data/hive/vendors.txt' INTO TABLE ven;`
`CREATE TABLE ven(id INT, name STRING) ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'; LOAD DATA INPATH '/data/hive/vendors.txt' INTO TABLE ven;`
`INSERT TABLE ven FROM '/data/hive/vendors.txt';`
`COPY ven FROM '/data/hive/vendors.txt' DELIMITER '\t';`
`BULK LOAD ven INFILE '/data/hive/vendors.txt';`

questions.explanation: A managed Hive table is created with plain `CREATE TABLE`, no EXTERNAL keyword, and the schema lists each column with its type. `ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'` tells Hive that fields are tab-separated. Because the source file is already in HDFS, `LOAD DATA INPATH` (without LOCAL) moves it into the managed table's warehouse directory. From then on, Hive owns the data and will delete it if the table is dropped. EXTERNAL tables leave data out of Hive's control, and INSERT TABLE FROM, COPY FROM, or BULK LOAD INFILE are not valid HiveQL commands, so those options are wrong.

questions.text: A Hive developer wants Hive to create partitions dynamically when inserting from a non-partitioned table `Logs_Raw` into a partitioned table `Logs_Part` partitioned by `EventType`. Which session setting must be applied BEFORE the INSERT?
options: `SET hive.mapred.mode = strict;`
`SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;`
`SET hive.enforce.bucketing = false;`
`SET hive.partition.disable = true;`
`SET hive.dynamic = off;`
questions.shortExplanation: `SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;` enables dynamic partitioning for the INSERT.
questions.explanation: Before an INSERT that wants Hive to create partitions automatically from a source column, the session must allow nonstrict dynamic partitioning. The command `SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;` removes the requirement that at least one partition column be static. questions.text: In Pig, a developer needs to load `/customers.csv` (comma-separated) and project only `custId` ($0) and `city` ($4). Which Pig Latin sequence is correct?

`cust = LOAD '/customers.csv' USING PigStorage(','); each_cust = FOREACH cust GENERATE $0 AS custId, $4 AS city;`
`cust = OPEN '/customers.csv'; FOREACH cust PROJECT $0, $4;`
`LOAD cust FROM '/customers.csv'; PROJECT $0, $4 INTO each_cust;`
`cust = IMPORT '/customers.csv'; each_cust = FILTER cust BY $0, $4;`

questions.text: A Pig script computes the SUM of `amount` per `accountId`. After `group_data = GROUP txns BY accountId;`, which FOREACH expression aggregates correctly?
options: `sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, COUNT(txns.amount);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, SUM(txns.amount);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE AVG(txns);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE FILTER(amount);`
`sum_data = FOREACH txns GENERATE SUM(group_data);`

questions.explanation: When a Pig relation is grouped, each row of the result has a `group` field with the key and an inner bag named after the original relation. To sum a column across that bag, use the SUM aggregate inside a FOREACH, like `SUM(time_sheet.miles_logged)`. The output gives one row per driver with their total miles, which is what the aggregation requires. Read both stores in parallel and return whichever responds last
Invalidate the Redis key on every read regardless of HIT/MISS

questions.text: A developer uploads `clickstream.csv` from the Linux shell into the HDFS directory `/lake/clicks`. Which command is correct?

questions.text: A DevOps engineer audits the number of blocks AND their physical DataNode locations for `/audits/system.log`. Which command returns BOTH?

`hdfs fsck /audits/system.log -files -blocks -locations`
`hdfs dfs -count /audits/system.log`

questions.text: A Hive developer wants Hive to create partitions dynamically when inserting from a non-partitioned table `Visits_Raw` into a partitioned table `Visits_Part` partitioned by `Country`. Which session setting must be applied BEFORE the INSERT?

questions.text: In Pig, a developer needs to load `/items.csv` (comma-separated) and project only `itemId` ($0) and `price` ($3). Which Pig Latin sequence is correct?

options: `sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, COUNT(sales.units_sold);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, SUM(sales.units_sold);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE AVG(sales);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE FILTER(units_sold);`
`sum_data = FOREACH sales GENERATE SUM(group_data);`

questions.explanation: When a Pig relation is grouped, each row of the result has a `group` field with the key and an inner bag named after the original relation. questions.text: A backend developer implements the standard "read-through cache" using Redis in front of a SQL database. A request arrives for `profile:emp9001`. Which logic correctly captures the pattern?

Bypass Redis on every read and use it only for writes
Read both stores in parallel and return whichever responds last
Invalidate the Redis key on every read regardless of HIT/MISS

questions.text: After a stock-level update in the source DB, customers continue seeing the old stock-status from Redis. Which Redis best-practice combination resolves this?

Set an appropriate TTL on the cached key AND invalidate/update the cache entry when the underlying DB row changes (via change-event triggers or Pub/Sub notifications)
Never invalidate; let data naturally drift
Use Redis only as a write-only store
Lower the TTL so far that every request becomes a miss, effectively bypassing the cache
questions.shortExplanation: Set a TTL on cached keys AND invalidate or update them when the DB row changes.
questions.explanation: Stale cache happens when the DB is updated but Redis still holds the old value. The fix is two-fold. Consumer pushes the message back to the Producer
The Queue produces messages and sends them to the Exchange

RabbitMQ — a message broker with Exchanges and bindings supporting flexible routing patterns, ideal for decoupling producer/consumer for async task distribution
Both are equivalent; the choice is irrelevant
Neither — only Redis Pub/Sub fits

Isolation

Availability

`CREATE TABLE br(id INT, name STRING) ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'; LOAD DATA INPATH '/data/hive/branches.txt' INTO TABLE br;`
`INSERT TABLE br FROM '/data/hive/branches.txt';`
`COPY br FROM '/data/hive/branches.txt' DELIMITER '\t';`

questions.text: A Hive developer wants Hive to create partitions dynamically when inserting from a non-partitioned table `Tickets_Raw` into a partitioned table `Tickets_Part` partitioned by `Priority`. Which session setting must be applied BEFORE the INSERT?

questions.text: In Pig, a developer needs to load `/courses.csv` (comma-separated) and project only `courseId` ($0) and `credits` ($2). Which Pig Latin sequence is correct?

questions.text: A backend developer implements the standard "read-through cache" using Redis in front of an SQL database. A request arrives for `subscription:uid7777`. Which logic correctly captures the pattern?

Read both stores in parallel and return whichever responds last
Invalidate the Redis key on every read regardless of HIT/MISS

questions.text: After a tariff plan change in the source DB, subscribers continue seeing the old plan price from Redis. Which Redis best-practice combination resolves this?

Set an appropriate TTL on the cached key AND invalidate/update the cache entry whenever the underlying DB row changes (via change-event triggers or Pub/Sub notifications)
Never invalidate; let data naturally drift
Use Redis only as a write-only store
Lower the TTL so far that every request becomes a miss, effectively bypassing the cache

questions.text: A real-time stock-ticker platform needs a pub-sub pipeline where price events are partitioned for horizontal scalability, every consumer group receives each message exactly once, ZooKeeper handles leader election, and messages survive broker failure via replication. Consumer pushes the message back to the Producer
The Queue produces messages and sends them to the Exchange
There is no broker — producer and consumer communicate directly

questions.text: An architect must choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ for a system needing FLEXIBLE message routing (direct, topic, fanout) and primarily distributing async tasks to specific worker queues rather than retaining a long event log for replay. Which fits best and why?

Neither — only Redis Pub/Sub fits

Durability
Availability

questions.text: The same team is told that once `commitTransaction()` returns success, changes must persist even if the DB server crashes moments later. Which ACID property guarantees this, and how should it be reasoned about in MongoDB?

Partition Tolerance — because the network was healthy

`COPY sn FROM '/data/hive/sensors.txt' DELIMITER '\t';`
`BULK LOAD sn INFILE '/data/hive/sensors.txt';`
questions.shortExplanation: Use `CREATE TABLE ... ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY` and then `LOAD DATA INPATH` for a managed table.
questions.explanation: A managed Hive table is created with plain `CREATE TABLE`, no EXTERNAL keyword, and the schema lists each column with its type. `ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY '\t'` tells Hive that fields are tab-separated. Because the source file is already in HDFS, `LOAD DATA INPATH` (without LOCAL) moves it into the managed table's warehouse directory. From then on, Hive owns the data and will delete it if the table is dropped. EXTERNAL tables leave data out of Hive's control, and INSERT TABLE FROM, COPY FROM, or BULK LOAD INFILE are not valid HiveQL commands, so those options are wrong.

questions.text: A Hive developer wants Hive to create partitions dynamically when inserting from a non-partitioned table `Alerts_Raw` into a partitioned table `Alerts_Part` partitioned by `Severity`. Which session setting must be applied BEFORE the INSERT?
options: `SET hive.mapred.mode = strict;`
`SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;`
`SET hive.enforce.bucketing = false;`
`SET hive.partition.disable = true;`
`SET hive.dynamic = off;`
questions.shortExplanation: `SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;` enables dynamic partitioning for the INSERT.
questions.explanation: Before an INSERT that wants Hive to create partitions automatically from a source column, the session must allow nonstrict dynamic partitioning. The command `SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;` removes the requirement that at least one partition column be static. With dynamic partitioning enabled, Hive reads each row, looks at the partition column value, and writes the row into the matching partition directory. Setting strict mode blocks fully dynamic inserts, disabling bucketing is unrelated, and properties like `hive.partition.disable` or `hive.dynamic=off` are made up, so those options will not work.

questions.text: In Pig, a developer needs to load `/farms.csv` (comma-separated) and project only `farmId` ($0) and `yieldKg` ($5). Which Pig Latin sequence is correct?
options: `farms = READ '/farms.csv' DELIMITER ','; SELECT $0, $5 FROM farms;`
`farms = LOAD '/farms.csv' USING PigStorage(','); each_farm = FOREACH farms GENERATE $0 AS farmId, $5 AS yieldKg;`
`farms = OPEN '/farms.csv'; FOREACH farms PROJECT $0, $5;`
`LOAD farms FROM '/farms.csv'; PROJECT $0, $5 INTO each_farm;`
`farms = IMPORT '/farms.csv'; each_farm = FILTER farms BY $0, $5;`
questions.shortExplanation: Use `LOAD ... USING PigStorage(',')` then `FOREACH ... GENERATE $0, $1` to project columns.
questions.explanation: Pig reads delimited files with `LOAD '<path>' USING PigStorage(',')`, where PigStorage tells Pig the field separator. The result is a relation of tuples whose positional columns are accessed as `$0`, `$1`, and so on. To project only the first two columns and rename them, use `FOREACH drivers GENERATE $0 AS driverId, $1 AS name;`. This is the standard load-then-project pattern in Pig Latin. Commands like READ, OPEN, IMPORT, PROJECT, or SELECT are not Pig Latin keywords, and FILTER is used for predicates not projection, so those options will not parse.

questions.text: A Pig script computes the SUM of `kwh_consumed` per `meterId`. After `group_data = GROUP usage BY meterId;`, which FOREACH expression aggregates correctly?
options: `sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, COUNT(usage.kwh_consumed);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, SUM(usage.kwh_consumed);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE AVG(usage);`
`sum_data = FOREACH group_data GENERATE FILTER(kwh_consumed);`
`sum_data = FOREACH usage GENERATE SUM(group_data);`
questions.shortExplanation: After GROUP BY, use `FOREACH group_data GENERATE group, SUM(time_sheet.miles_logged)` to total miles.
questions.explanation: When a Pig relation is grouped, each row of the result has a `group` field with the key and an inner bag named after the original relation. To sum a column across that bag, use the SUM aggregate inside a FOREACH, like `SUM(time_sheet.miles_logged)`. The output gives one row per driver with their total miles, which is what the aggregation requires. COUNT only counts rows, AVG computes mean not sum, FILTER does not aggregate, and applying SUM to the original ungrouped relation does not produce per-driver totals.

questions.text: A backend developer implements the standard "read-through cache" using Redis in front of an SQL database. A request arrives for `student:s10042`. Which logic correctly captures the pattern?
options: Always read the SQL DB first; optionally update Redis later
Look up `student:s10042` in Redis; on HIT return cached value; on MISS read from SQL DB, write the result back into Redis with a TTL, and return the data
Bypass Redis on every read and use it only for writes
Read both stores in parallel and return whichever responds last
Invalidate the Redis key on every read regardless of HIT/MISS
questions.shortExplanation: Read-through cache: check Redis first; on HIT return it, on MISS read DB, write back to Redis, return.
questions.explanation: The read-through pattern wraps every read in a small piece of logic. The app first asks Redis for the key. If Redis returns a value (HIT), the app uses it immediately. If Redis says the key is missing (MISS), the app queries the relational DB, writes the result back into Redis with a TTL, and returns it to the caller. Subsequent reads of the same key now hit Redis and avoid the DB, which is exactly the goal of caching. Always reading DB first, bypassing Redis, reading both in parallel, or invalidating on every read all defeat the purpose of a cache and would lose its latency benefits.

questions.text: After a course-fee update in the source DB, students continue seeing the old fee from Redis. Which Redis best-practice combination resolves this?
options: Disable Redis and serve all reads from the DB
Set an appropriate TTL on the cached key AND invalidate/update the cache entry when the underlying DB row changes (via change-event triggers or Pub/Sub notifications)
Never invalidate; let data naturally drift
Use Redis only as a write-only store
Lower the TTL so far that every request becomes a miss, effectively bypassing the cache
questions.shortExplanation: Set a TTL on cached keys AND invalidate or update them when the DB row changes.
questions.explanation: Stale cache happens when the DB is updated but Redis still holds the old value. The fix is two-fold. First, every cached key gets a Time-To-Live so it expires and is naturally refreshed after a known window. Second, when the underlying DB row changes, the app or a change-event hook (such as a Pub/Sub trigger) invalidates or updates the corresponding Redis key right away. Together these keep the cache from drifting too far from the source of truth. Disabling Redis kills its benefit, never invalidating guarantees stale data, write-only Redis is meaningless for reads, and a TTL of zero turns every request into a miss and removes the cache.

questions.text: A real-time SOC platform needs a pub-sub pipeline where security events are partitioned for horizontal scalability, every consumer group receives each message exactly once, ZooKeeper handles leader election, and messages survive broker failure via replication. Which technology stack fits and what is each component's role?
options: RabbitMQ — producers send directly to consumers without partitions

Apache Kafka — producers publish to topics (partitioned for scalability), brokers store and replicate data across the cluster for fault tolerance, consumer groups read with once-only processing per message, and ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata and leader election
Redis — Redis is a stream-only system with no partitions
Kubernetes — Kubernetes is the underlying messaging system
MongoDB ACID transactions as the message bus
questions.shortExplanation: Kafka topics are partitioned for scale, brokers replicate them, consumer groups read once per message, ZooKeeper coordinates brokers.
questions.explanation: Producers publish events into named Kafka topics, and each topic is divided into partitions so messages can be spread across brokers for horizontal scalability. Brokers store the partition logs and replicate them across the cluster so a broker failure does not lose data. Consumers join a consumer group, and each partition is assigned to one consumer in the group, which gives exactly-once-per-group processing. ZooKeeper coordinates broker metadata, leader election, and consumer offsets in older versions. RabbitMQ has no partitions, Redis is not a partitioned event log, Kubernetes is not a messaging system, and MongoDB ACID is a database, so none of them match this architecture.

questions.text: A web app must offload heavy certificate-generation so user requests stay fast. The team adopts RabbitMQ. Which sequence correctly captures the RabbitMQ workflow per the slides?
options: Producer → Queue → Exchange → Consumer
Producer (web app) sends a message to an Exchange, which routes it (via bindings and routing keys) to a Queue, where it waits until a Consumer (worker) connects and processes it
Consumer pushes the message back to the Producer
The Queue produces messages and sends them to the Exchange
There is no broker — producer and consumer communicate directly
questions.shortExplanation: RabbitMQ flow: Producer → Exchange → (routing rules) → Queue → Consumer.
questions.explanation: In RabbitMQ, a producer never sends messages directly to a queue. It publishes to an Exchange and includes a routing key or attributes. The exchange uses its bindings (direct, topic, fanout, headers) to decide which queues should receive the message. A consumer subscribes to one of those queues and processes messages as they arrive. This decoupling allows the producer to be unaware of which workers will handle the work. Other orderings, having the consumer push back to the producer, or claiming there is no broker contradict how RabbitMQ actually routes messages.

questions.text: An architect must choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ for a system needing FLEXIBLE message routing (direct, topic, fanout) and primarily distributing async tasks to specific worker queues rather than retaining a long event log for replay. Which fits best and why?
options: Kafka — because Kafka has Exchanges built for task queues
RabbitMQ — a message broker with Exchanges and bindings supporting flexible routing patterns, ideal for decoupling producer/consumer for async task distribution
Both are equivalent; the choice is irrelevant
Neither — only Redis Pub/Sub fits
Use Kubernetes; it natively routes messages
questions.shortExplanation: Pick RabbitMQ when you need flexible exchange-based routing and reliable async task delivery.
questions.explanation: RabbitMQ is the right tool for systems where work must be reliably handed off from producers to specific worker queues, and where routing rules vary by message type. Exchanges support direct, topic, and fanout routing patterns that let one publish reach exactly the queues that need it. It is not built to retain a long event log for replay, which is what Kafka is for. PDF generation and bulk email sending are textbook RabbitMQ workloads. Kafka does not use exchanges, claiming the two are equivalent ignores their core design difference, Redis Pub/Sub does not give durable task delivery, and Kubernetes does not route application messages.

questions.text: A campus billing service implements a tuition payment that must (1) debit student wallet, (2) credit the institute account, and (3) write a fee-record row — all three or none. The team wraps these in a MongoDB multi-document ACID transaction. Which ACID property provides the "or none" guarantee?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity — all operations succeed together, or none are applied; partial updates are prevented
Durability
Availability
questions.shortExplanation: Atomicity guarantees that all operations in a transaction succeed together or none are applied.
questions.explanation: In a MongoDB multi-document transaction, Atomicity treats the whole transaction as one indivisible unit. Either every write inside it commits, or if anything fails the database rolls back all of them, leaving the data exactly as it was before. This stops half-finished outcomes such as a debit without a credit, which would corrupt account balances. Atomicity is enforced through the commit and abort protocol around the wrapped operations. Consistency is about constraints, Isolation is about concurrent visibility, Durability is about surviving crashes after commit, and Availability is not even an ACID property, so they do not describe all-or-nothing behavior.

questions.text: The same team is told that once `commitTransaction()` returns success, changes must persist even if the DB host crashes seconds later. Which ACID property guarantees this, and how should it be reasoned about in MongoDB?
options: Atomicity — because the operation is indivisible
Isolation — because other transactions cannot see partial state
Durability — once a transaction commits successfully, its effects are persisted permanently and survive crashes, restarts, and power failures
Consistency — because constraints were respected
Partition Tolerance — because the network was healthy
questions.shortExplanation: Durability means the committed transaction's effects survive crashes, restarts, and power failures.
questions.explanation: Once `commitTransaction()` returns success in MongoDB, Durability promises that the change is now safely on disk in the journal and replicas. Even if the server power-cycles a millisecond later, the data is recovered on restart. MongoDB achieves this with journaling and write-concern majority, which forces the commit to be acknowledged on multiple nodes before returning success. Without Durability, a successful commit could be lost, breaking trust in the system. Atomicity is about indivisibility, Isolation is about concurrent access, Consistency is about constraints, and Partition Tolerance belongs to CAP not ACID, so they do not describe crash survival of committed data.

questions.text: A DevOps engineer writes a Kubernetes YAML manifest declaring "12 replicas of telemetry-svc with image telemetry:1.2". After applying it, four Pods are evicted due to node maintenance. Kubernetes immediately starts four new Pods to maintain 12 replicas. Which TWO K8s capabilities does this MOST directly illustrate?
options: Declarative configuration (desired state in YAML) + Self-healing (controller reconciles actual state to desired state)
Manual SSH + Hand-edited routing tables
Vertical scaling + Static IP assignment
Database replication + Cache eviction
Kafka partitioning + RabbitMQ exchanges
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes uses declarative YAML for desired state and a self-healing controller loop to maintain it.
questions.explanation: A Kubernetes manifest expresses what the user wants — for example, three replicas of an nginx Pod — and submits it to the API Server. Controllers then continuously compare the actual cluster state to that desired state. If a Pod dies, the ReplicaSet controller notices the mismatch and starts a new Pod automatically, bringing the count back to three. This combination of declarative configuration and a self-healing reconcile loop is the heart of how Kubernetes operates. Manual SSH, hard-coded IPs, vertical scaling only, plain DB replication, or Kafka and RabbitMQ features are not what this YAML-plus-controller behavior demonstrates.

questions.text: A microservices team runs 45 services on Kubernetes. As traffic grows, they need automatic scaling and traffic routed to new replicas without hand-editing config. Which K8s feature set matches?
options: Manual port-forwarding and hand-edited hosts files
Horizontal scaling (add Pods/Nodes) combined with Service Discovery and Load Balancing — services locate each other dynamically and traffic is distributed across replicas
Vertical scaling only — adding RAM to a single Pod
Disable autoscaling and rely on a single replica per service
Move everything off Kubernetes and back onto bare VMs
questions.shortExplanation: Horizontal scaling plus Service Discovery and Load Balancing let new Pods receive traffic automatically.
questions.explanation: When a microservice needs more capacity, Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can add more Pods. Each Service object gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP that automatically tracks the set of healthy Pods behind it. kube-proxy programs network rules so that traffic to the service is load-balanced across all current replicas. New Pods are discovered and added to the rotation without anyone editing config files by hand. Manual port-forwarding, single-replica setups, vertical-only scaling, and moving off Kubernetes all defeat the very automation the team is trying to use.

questions.text: A team needs Redis to absorb >800K req/sec — more than one instance can handle. Which Redis scaling strategy aligns with what was taught?
options: Vertical scaling only — buy a bigger Redis box
Use Redis Clusters or replication to distribute data across multiple instances and increase throughput
Run Redis on a developer laptop in dev mode
Disable Redis and use a relational DB
Use Kafka instead of Redis since Redis cannot scale
questions.shortExplanation: Use Redis Clusters or replication to spread data and serve more than a single instance can handle.
questions.explanation: A single Redis instance has a CPU and memory ceiling, so to push beyond it Redis offers two scaling tools. Redis Cluster shards keys across multiple primary nodes, increasing throughput and capacity together. Replication adds replicas to a primary so read traffic can be served from several nodes and failover is possible if the primary dies. Together they let Redis scale horizontally to hundreds of thousands of requests per second. Sticking to one bigger server eventually hits the same ceiling, dev-mode laptops are toys, replacing Redis with an RDBMS loses the low-latency benefit, and Kafka is not a cache replacement.

questions.text: A Kafka consumer group on the `audit-events` topic must REPLAY messages from an earlier point to rebuild a downstream compliance database corrupted yesterday. Which Kafka concept enables this?
options: Kafka deletes messages immediately on consumption — replay is impossible
Consumers can choose any OFFSET within the topic's retention window — Kafka retains messages for a configured period, enabling replay
Only Kafka producers can read past messages, not consumers
RabbitMQ must be installed alongside Kafka for replay
Replay requires shutting down the entire Kafka cluster
questions.shortExplanation: Kafka retains messages for a configured period and lets consumers seek to any offset within it to replay.
questions.explanation: Each Kafka topic partition is an append-only log where every message has an offset. Kafka keeps the messages for as long as the retention configuration allows, regardless of whether anyone has consumed them. A consumer can rewind its committed offset, or set a fresh starting offset such as `earliest`, to replay past messages and reprocess them — which is how teams recover from downstream bugs without producing the events again. Saying Kafka deletes messages instantly, restricting reads to producers, claiming RabbitMQ is required, or demanding a full cluster shutdown all contradict how Kafka offsets and retention actually work.

questions.text: A startup runs an interbank settlement service requiring strong consistency and rollback on failure, plus a public live-poll-results service that prioritizes availability and tolerates eventual consistency. Which architectural pairing matches the ACID-vs-BASE comparison taught?
options: Settlement → BASE; Poll-results → ACID
Settlement → ACID (strong consistency, transactional rollback, durability); Poll-results → BASE (eventual consistency, high availability, relaxed durability)
Both should use BASE because ACID is impossible in distributed systems
Both should use ACID since BASE is always unsafe
Settlement → no DB at all; Poll-results → ACID only
questions.shortExplanation: Use ACID for strong, consistent transactional systems and BASE for highly available, eventually consistent feeds.
questions.explanation: ACID databases give strong consistency, transactional rollback, and durability, which is exactly what a banking application needs so it never shows partial transfers. BASE systems prioritize availability and partition tolerance, accepting that replicas may briefly disagree before converging — perfect for a social-media feed where users tolerate seeing slightly stale posts in exchange for the service never being down. Choosing the right side per workload is a core distributed-systems decision. Swapping the two would put feed data on a slow strict system and money on an eventually consistent one, and claims like 'ACID is impossible' or 'BASE is unsafe' overstate the trade-off.

questions.text: A Kubernetes cluster has a Control Plane plus nine Worker Nodes. Each Worker Node runs Pods plus two helper components. Which TWO components run on EACH Worker Node, and what do they do (per the K8s architecture taught)?
options: API Server (handles requests) and etcd (stores cluster state)
kubelet (manages the Pods on the node and talks to the control plane) and kube-proxy (handles network rules and service routing for Pods)
Scheduler (places Pods) and Controller Manager (reconciles state)
ZooKeeper and Kafka Broker
Redis Cluster and RabbitMQ Exchange
questions.shortExplanation: Each Worker Node runs `kubelet` (manages Pods on the node) and `kube-proxy` (handles network routing for services).
questions.explanation: On every Kubernetes Worker Node two helper components run alongside the user Pods. The `kubelet` talks to the control plane, starts and supervises containers in Pods, and reports node and Pod health back to the API Server. `kube-proxy` programs the node's iptables or IPVS rules so traffic for a Service is correctly load-balanced to the right Pod IPs. Together they implement the worker side of the Kubernetes architecture. API Server, etcd, Scheduler, and Controller Manager are control-plane components, while ZooKeeper, Kafka, Redis, and RabbitMQ are entirely different products, so none of them run on a Worker Node by default.
